rationale: Both headings present wisdom speech through a son of David who reigns in Israel; the parallel identifies a literary royal setting without proving identical authorship.
The opening declaration that everything is futility returns at the close with the same attribution to Ecclesiastes, framing the intervening investigation.
Both ask what surplus the worker obtains from toil, making the later question a return to the book's opening problem.
Passing human generations are set against the enduring earth in the source; the psalm contrasts passing human lives with God's endurance across generations.
The sun travels toward its place in the source; the psalm depicts its course from one edge of heaven to the other.
The wind repeatedly returns on its circuits, providing a concrete natural example of the later claim that what has happened will happen again.
Streams continually return to their course without filling the sea, illustrating the chapter's subsequent description of repeated happenings beneath the sun.
The source's eye is never filled with seeing; the proverb likewise calls human eyes insatiable, supporting the shared observation about unfulfilled desire.
Both collapse the distinction between past and future by saying that what will happen has already happened.
The imagined announcement of something new is answered by appeal to earlier ages, elaborating the preceding denial of anything fresh beneath the sun.
The general disappearance of earlier generations from memory becomes the more particular claim that neither wise nor foolish people retain enduring remembrance.
The first-person declaration of kingship in Jerusalem takes up the royal identity supplied by the chapter's opening heading.
God-given human distraction appears in both passages; the target adds that people cannot discover God's whole work despite their inquiry.
The sweeping judgment of works beneath the sun as futility and resolve of spirit returns after the speaker examines his own achievements.
Both deny human power to put what is twisted in order; the later saying explicitly situates the difficulty within God's works.
The speaker claims wisdom surpassing earlier Jerusalem figures; God's promise to Solomon likewise describes a wise heart without a comparable predecessor or successor.
Both describe deliberately seeking wisdom and knowledge; the later search extends the inquiry explicitly to an ungodly person's folly, continuing and broadening the opening experiment.
Increasing knowledge increases pain in the source; the closing warning similarly recognizes bodily weariness from much study.
The experiment with gladness proves futile; the later comparison of foolish laughter with crackling thorns likewise ends by declaring futility.
Calling laughter delirium anticipates the later preference for mourning and wise rebuke over the gladness, songs and laughter of fools.
The experiment asks what people should do during their numbered days; the target asks who knows what is good during those same limited days.
The source lists building houses among royal projects; the Kings unit explicitly includes the king's house and extensive building undertakings.
The source's acquired slaves belong to its account of royal possessions; Kings distinguishes subjected peoples and Israelites' royal service, supplying a concrete parallel for organized royal labor.
The source accumulates silver, gold and riches of kings and regions; Kings records Solomon's gold receipts and tribute from regional kings and officials.
The speaker combines surpassing greatness with retained wisdom; Kings likewise combines Solomon's surpassing wealth with surpassing discernment.
Joy in the speaker's toil is called his portion; the target likewise locates a person's portion in rejoicing in his works.
The source finds no surplus in its completed works; Paul, after discussing resurrection, assures believers that their labor in the Lord is not empty.
The advantage of wisdom over folly is pictured as light over darkness; Proverbs contrasts illuminated righteous ways with dark ways that cause stumbling.
The source acknowledges one event for wise and foolish people; the later passage expands the same observation across righteous, ungodly and other contrasting groups.
The speaker questions wisdom because he shares the fool's fate; the following verse specifies their shared death and absence of enduring remembrance.

relationship: parallel death of wise and foolish
rationale: The source brings wise and foolish people together in death; the psalm likewise speaks of wise people dying and foolish people perishing.
The speaker hates life because its work is grievous; Job's lament likewise prefers having died immediately and found rest to his present suffering.

relationship: parallel loss of labors to an heir
rationale: Both expressly describe leaving one's labors to another, with Sirach naming the division of an inheritance.
The source cannot know the character of the person who will control its toil; the parable asks whose the stored goods will be when their owner dies.
The speaker's withdrawal of heart from toil follows the stated distress that another person, possibly foolish, will control everything produced.
The source calls it grievous to give one's hard-won portion to someone who did not labor; Sirach similarly anticipates one's labors becoming another's inheritance.
Both ask what a person obtains from all the toil undertaken beneath the sun, repeating the book's governing question.
The source's toiling heart cannot sleep at night; the later contrast says that abundance of riches prevents sleep even while the worker sleeps sweetly.
Both explicitly locate eating, drinking and seeing goodness in one's toil in God's giving, rather than treating enjoyment as self-produced.
The question about eating apart from God is developed by the statement that God must empower a person to eat from his possessions.

relationship: parallel divine gift of wisdom and prosperity
rationale: The source attributes wisdom, knowledge and gladness to God's giving; Kings depicts God giving Solomon discernment, wealth and glory.
The source assigns a time and season to every matter; Daniel explicitly places changes of seasons and times under God's action.
The source places birth and death in paired times; Hannah's prayer pairs the Lord's putting to death and giving life, grounding the contrast in divine action.
The source pairs pulling down with building; Jeremiah's commission likewise includes demolishing and building among opposed appointed actions.
The source recognizes distinct times for weeping and laughter; Paul instructs believers to join others in rejoicing and weeping as their circumstances require.
The source distinguishes a time to be silent from a time to speak; Amos provides a particular case in which understanding calls for silence in an evil time.
The worker's surplus from toil restates the opening question about a person's surplus from labor beneath the sun.
Both passages identify the distracting human occupation being investigated as something God has given to human beings.
Humans cannot find God's work from beginning to end in the source; the target insists that even a wise person's searching cannot discover it.
The source finds good in rejoicing during life; the later passage praises gladness as accompanying one's toil through God-given days.
The source calls eating, drinking and enjoying one's toil God's gift; Paul describes God as richly providing things for enjoyment.
No addition or subtraction can be made to God's enduring work in the source; Deuteronomy forbids adding to or subtracting from God's command, applying completeness to His word.
The temporal claim that what will come has already happened repeats the earlier description of recurring events beneath the sun; the target does not address the pursued person.
Ungodliness occupies the place of judgment in the source; the target explicitly names robbery of judgment and righteousness alongside oppression of the poor.
The source expects God to judge righteous and ungodly people; the conclusion likewise brings every deed, good or evil, into God's judgment.
The source exposes human beings as beasts to themselves; the psalm similarly compares the uncomprehending person in honor with senseless beasts.
The source compares human and animal death; the psalm joins comparison with beasts to being placed like sheep in Hades under death's rule.
Both explicitly say that the human being returns to the earth from which he was taken, grounding mortality in earthly origin.
The source questions whether the human spirit goes upward; the closing passage says the spirit returns to God, without resolving the source's separate question about beasts.
Both call rejoicing in one's works or toil a person's portion, directing attention to present enjoyment of labor.
The source observes victims' tears and their oppressors' power; James depicts withheld wages crying out and a murdered righteous person offering no resistance.

relationship: parallel preference for death amid suffering
rationale: The source praises the already dead above the living; Job's lament imagines death as rest beyond present bodily exhaustion and servitude.

relationship: parallel preference for never experiencing life
rationale: The source prefers someone not yet born who has not seen evil; Job similarly imagines the condition of a miscarriage or infant who never saw light.
The source identifies rivalry with one's companion beneath productive toil; James connects jealousy and selfish ambition with disorder rather than wisdom from above.
The fool's folded hands lead to consuming his own flesh; Proverbs likewise connects clasped hands and inactivity with arriving poverty and want.
A handful of rest is preferred to doubled toil; Proverbs similarly prefers a small portion and friendly vegetables to greater stores and hostile feasting.
The isolated worker's eye is not filled with wealth; the later saying likewise states that loving silver never results in being filled with silver.
The assertion that two receive better reward is developed by specific benefits: lifting a fallen partner, providing warmth and resisting an opponent together.
A companion lifts the person who falls; Proverbs likewise describes friends and brothers as useful precisely in times of need.
Two can withstand an assailant where one cannot; Sirach describes a faithful friend as a strong shelter, giving a related protective account of friendship.
The poor wise youth is preferred to the foolish king; Proverbs likewise allows an intelligent servant to rule foolish masters, placing understanding above rank.

relationship: narrative parallel of elevation from confinement
rationale: The source pictures someone coming from confinement to rule; Joseph is brought from the fortress and, after his discerning counsel, appointed over Egypt. It is a parallel, not an identification.
The source urges approaching God's house to listen while criticizing fools' gifts; Samuel explicitly ranks listening and attentiveness above sacrifice.
The source calls for few words before God in heaven; Jesus rejects babbling many words and begins the model prayer by addressing the Father in heaven.
The source associates a fool's voice with many words; Proverbs warns that much talking does not escape sin and commends restraint of the lips.
Both command someone who vows to God not to delay paying the vow; the Deuteronomy passage explicitly makes failure sinful.
The source prefers abstaining from a vow to failing to pay; Deuteronomy expressly says there is no sin in choosing not to vow.
The source refuses an excuse of ignorance for a mouth that incurs sin; Deuteronomy requires doing what one's lips have spoken as a gift vowed to God.
Fear of God answers the source's abundance of futile dreams and words; the same imperative governs the book's concluding summary.
The source names extortion of the poor and stolen justice; James depicts withheld laborers' wages together with condemnation and murder of a righteous person.
The silver lover is never filled with silver; Proverbs likewise presents human eyes as insatiable, describing the appetite that possession does not satisfy.
Increasing goods leaves their owner merely looking while others consume; the target likewise describes possessions from which a stranger, rather than the owner, eats.
Riches prevent their owner's sleep in the source; the earlier account of painful toil likewise leaves the heart awake at night.
Wealth is kept to its owner's harm; Paul describes the desire for riches and love of money leading people into ruin and many pains.
The source depicts wealth disappearing and leaving a son empty-handed; Paul's warning against hoping in uncertain wealth states the principle illustrated by that loss.
Both describe coming naked from the mother's womb and departing naked, using the same birth-and-departure comparison to deny lasting possession.

relationship: parallel inability to carry wealth away
rationale: The source says a person departs as he came despite toil; Paul likewise says people brought nothing into the world and can carry nothing out.
The source's days of darkness, mourning and anger recall the earlier description of all one's days as pain and one's distraction as anger.
Both commend eating, drinking and seeing goodness in one's toil within God's provision, giving the same practical response to labor's limits.
God both grants possessions and enables their enjoyment in the source; Paul directs the wealthy toward God as the provider of things for enjoyment.
God occupies the person's heart with gladness; the later saying describes rejoicing as accompanying a person through the days God gives.

relationship: explicit contrast in enjoyment of wealth
rationale: Both describe God-given possessions, but the source denies the owner power to eat while the earlier passage makes that power a further gift from God.

relationship: parallel preference for a stillborn condition
rationale: The source prefers a stillborn child to long life without goodness; Job likewise imagines rest through death at birth or the condition of a miscarriage.
The source's stillborn child has not seen the sun yet has more rest; Job joins imagined rest in death to infants who never saw light.
Even greatly prolonged life ends at the one place in the source; the earlier passage explicitly says all go to one place and return to dust.
The source says labor feeds the mouth without filling appetite; Proverbs similarly characterizes human eyes as insatiable, emphasizing desire's persistence.
The question about the wise person's advantage over the fool resumes the earlier tension between wisdom's benefit and the death shared by wise and foolish alike.
The source prefers what the eyes actually see to wandering appetite; Paul similarly commends contentment with present food and coverings.

relationship: parallel inability to contend with superior power
rationale: The source denies a human being's ability to contend in judgment with one stronger; Job expressly denies successful litigation or resistance against the mighty Lord.
Many words increase futility in the source; Proverbs warns that much talking fails to escape sin and instead commends restrained lips.

relationship: shared ignorance and brevity of life
rationale: The source asks who knows life's good or future and likens life to a shadow; James combines ignorance of tomorrow with the image of a disappearing vapor.

relationship: parallel value of a good name
rationale: The source prefers a name to good oil; Proverbs likewise values a good name above great wealth and favor above silver and gold.
The house of mourning makes the living take everyone's end to heart; Sirach similarly instructs remembering one's last things as a guard against sin.
A troubled face can improve the heart in the source; the psalmist likewise calls humiliation good because it taught him God's ordinances.
The contrast between wise hearts in mourning and fools in gladness rests on the earlier explanation that mourning makes the living take mortality to heart.
The source prefers hearing wise rebuke to fools' singing; Proverbs pictures a wise word fitting a receptive ear like a precious ornament.
The source compares foolish laughter to the sound of thorns beneath a cauldron and calls it futility; the earlier experiment similarly labels laughter delirium and questions gladness.
Extortion drives the wise astray and destroys their heart in the source; Proverbs likewise says receiving bribes destroys the taker.
The source ranks a patient person above someone high in spirit; Proverbs likewise places patience and control of anger above physical and military power.
The source forbids haste to anger because anger lodges with fools; James commands slowness to anger because human anger fails to accomplish God's righteousness.
Wisdom is good alongside an inheritance in the source; Wisdom of Solomon similarly joins good things and wealth to wisdom while treating her as their guide.
The source compares wisdom's shelter with silver but gives life-giving advantage to wisdom; the target likewise values wisdom above wealth and calls her an unfailing treasure.
The source asks who can put in order what God has twisted; the earlier proverb similarly states that what is twisted cannot be put in order.
God makes differing days while concealing what comes afterward in the source; the earlier passage joins God's fitting ordering of times to humanity's inability to discover His whole work.
The source observes righteousness ending in death while evil continues; the psalm likewise juxtaposes prospering sinners with the righteous speaker's persistent affliction.

The source's warning against being excessively wise is compared with Sirach's prohibition on investigating beyond human strength; this addresses the wisdom clause without equating righteousness with sin.

relationship: parallel warning about ungodliness and lifespan
rationale: The source warns that great ungodliness may bring death before one's time; the later saying denies the ungodly lasting good and prolonged days.
Holding to both warnings refers to the preceding cautions against excessive righteousness or wisdom and great ungodliness; fearing God supplies the stated way through both dangers.

relationship: parallel superiority of wisdom to force
rationale: Wisdom helps more than ten city rulers in the source; Proverbs prefers wisdom to strength and associates successful warfare with deliberation.
The source denies an earthly righteous person who never sins; Paul likewise charges all with sin and cites the absence of even one righteous person.
The instruction not to attend to every spoken insult is grounded in the following reminder that the hearer has also cursed others.
The source recalls one's own curses when hurt by another's speech; Jesus likewise requires attention to one's own fault before correcting another's.
The resolve to become wise and test matters by wisdom resumes the earlier determination to know wisdom and understanding.
Wisdom has withdrawn into an unfathomable depth in the source; Job asks where wisdom can be found and has the abyss deny possessing it.
The source continues the earlier intentional pursuit of wisdom and knowledge, now explicitly extending its inquiry to an ungodly person's folly, harshness and delirium.
The source depicts a woman as nets and bonds catching the sinner; Proverbs depicts seductive speech as snares leading the victim toward slaughter and Hades.
The source distinguishes God's upright creation of humanity from later human reasonings; Genesis depicts male and female humanity within the creation God judges very good.
The source asks who knows the solution of a saying; Proverbs describes discerning people learning to understand obscure sayings and riddles.

relationship: related care over words sworn to God
rationale: The source warns against haste concerning an oath of God; the earlier instructions require payment of vows and refuse excuses for rashly spoken obligations.
The warning about standing in an evil matter is followed by the explanation that a king speaks with authority and resists questioning, clarifying the practical danger.

relationship: contrast between royal and divine authority
rationale: The source presents the king's word as difficult to challenge; Daniel places kings beneath God, who transfers and appoints them, qualifying that earthly authority.
The wise heart knows a time of judgment; the earlier passage likewise joins God's judgment of righteous and ungodly people to a time for every work.
The source's assertion that every matter has a time and judgment repeats the earlier premise that every matter beneath heaven has its season.
Both say a person does not know what will follow and ask who can tell him, restating the limit on human foresight.
No one controls the day of death in the source; Hebrews likewise treats dying as an appointment for human beings and places judgment after it.
The source explicitly sees one person's authority harming another; the earlier scene depicts power in oppressors' hands and tears among those without comfort.
Public praise for the ungodly anticipates the later complaint that ungodly people receive outcomes appropriate to righteous deeds.
The source describes people emboldened in evil when no prompt opposition comes; Paul warns that despising divine forbearance stores up future wrath rather than granting impunity.
The sinner's apparent length of days is balanced by assurance for those who fear God; the following verse denies lasting good to the ungodly who lack that fear.
The source denies lasting good and prolonged days to the ungodly; the psalm portrays an exalted ungodly person vanishing and contrasts him with the peaceful person's remnant.
The source complains that righteous and ungodly people receive each other's expected outcomes; the psalm contrasts thriving sinners with the righteous speaker's daily affliction.
Both commend eating, drinking and rejoicing amid toil through the limited days God has given beneath the sun.
The speaker again sets his heart to know wisdom and inspect earthly distraction, resuming the inquiry first announced over everything beneath heaven.

relationship: repeated inability to discover God's work
rationale: Both explicitly deny human access to the whole of God's work; the source intensifies this by including the wise person's unsuccessful searching.
Both place the righteous in God's hand; Wisdom of Solomon develops that image into peace and hope of immortality despite appearances of death.
One event comes to all the source's morally and ritually distinct groups; the earlier passage makes the same observation about wise and foolish people.

relationship: parallel pervasive evil of the heart
rationale: The source describes human hearts as full of evil during life; Genesis likewise describes continual human inclination of the heart toward evil.
The living person's hope, illustrated by a living dog over a dead lion, is followed by the contrast between living awareness and the dead's lost knowledge and reward.

relationship: parallel cessation of thought at death
rationale: The source says the dead know nothing and lose remembrance; the psalm likewise describes a departing spirit and the perishing of the person's reasonings that day.

relationship: same-chapter limit on participation after death
rationale: The dead lose their share in earthly activity in the source; the later exhortation grounds present action in the absence of deed, knowledge and wisdom in Hades.

relationship: repeated joyful eating under divine favor
rationale: The source commends glad eating and drinking under God's favor; the earlier passage calls eating, drinking and seeing good in toil God's gift.
The source urges enjoying life with the woman one loves; Proverbs likewise commands shared joy and continuing affectionate companionship with one's own wife.
The source commands energetic work before the inactivity of Hades; Jesus likewise urges doing the sender's works while it is day, before night prevents work.
The source denies that might guarantees victory; the psalm likewise denies salvation through an army's size, a giant's strength or a horse's power.
The source pictures an unexpected evil time trapping people suddenly; the rich fool is abruptly told that his soul is demanded that very night.

relationship: narrative parallel of a besieged city
rationale: The source describes siegeworks raised against a small city; Samuel likewise records a siege mound and an army preparing to breach a city's wall.

relationship: narrative parallel of wisdom delivering a city
rationale: A poor wise man saves the source's city; in Samuel a wise woman's negotiation ends the siege. The comparison concerns civic rescue through wisdom, not identical actors or outcomes of remembrance.

relationship: parallel superiority of wisdom to strength
rationale: The source explicitly prefers wisdom to strength, though the poor wise person is despised; Proverbs similarly calls a wise person better than a strong one.
After noting that a poor wise person's words go unheard, the source values quietly heard wisdom above rulers' shouting, correcting the preference for social power over counsel.
Wisdom is better than weapons of war in the source; Proverbs illustrates that advantage through a wise person bringing down an impious stronghold.

Death-bringing flies spoil fragrant oil in the source; the preceding chapter likewise says one sinner destroys much good. The comparison concerns the damage image, not a reversal of the source's praise of little wisdom.
Right and left distinguish wise and foolish hearts in the source; Proverbs likewise distinguishes good and evil ways through contrasting light and darkness.
The fool's road-going and considerations expose his lack of heart; Proverbs likewise describes the person lacking understanding as led by foolishness instead of wisdom.
The source counsels steadiness and healing when an authority's spirit rises; Proverbs similarly says a yielding answer turns away wrath.
The source calls the elevation of a fool an evil; Proverbs likewise says luxury does not benefit a fool and criticizes a servant's insolent rule.

relationship: contrast in reversal of social rank
rationale: The source places mounted slaves above walking rulers within a complaint about misrule; Proverbs gives a contrasting, wisdom-based reason for a servant to rule foolish masters.
Both say that the one who digs a pit falls into it; Proverbs explicitly frames the pit as intended for a neighbor and adds a rebounding stone.

relationship: repeated advantage of wisdom over force
rationale: After a difficulty involving iron and strengthening forces, the source identifies wisdom as the courageous person's advantage; the earlier saying directly prefers wisdom to strength.
The source says a fool's lips drown him; Proverbs likewise calls the fool's mouth his ruin and his lips a trap for his life.
Speech moving from folly to evil wandering explains the preceding statement that the fool's own lips bring him down.
The fool multiplies words despite ignorance of what follows; the earlier passage likewise joins many futile words to the question of who can disclose the future.
The fool unable to find the city recalls the earlier fool walking along the road without understanding, giving practical form to the chapter's portrayal of folly.
The woe against a young king and rulers feasting in the morning is answered by blessing a land with a freeborn king and rulers who eat at the proper time.
The source blesses a land with disciplined rulers; Proverbs likewise credits a righteous king with raising up a country, in contrast to lawless destruction.
Idle hands allow a house to leak and its roof to sink; Proverbs likewise connects prolonged inactivity with the arrival of poverty and want.

relationship: shared disclosure principle in different settings
rationale: The source warns that even private curses may be reported; Jesus likewise says hidden things will become known, though His setting concerns fearless witness rather than courtly caution.
Bread sent upon water is found after many days; Jesus likewise depicts giving as followed by return. This comparison does not settle whether the source pictures commerce or generosity.
Sharing among seven and eight is urged because future evil is unknown; sowing morning and evening similarly spreads effort because the successful outcome is unknown.
Watching uncertain weather prevents sowing and reaping; the later command instead urges repeated sowing despite not knowing which effort will succeed.

relationship: shared hidden formation in the womb
rationale: The source compares unknowable divine work to bones in a pregnant womb; the psalm describes God knowing and forming hidden bones and unworked substance before birth.
The source urges continued sowing because success is uncertain; Paul likewise urges perseverance but promises a harvest for doing good without giving up.

relationship: literary contrast of light and decline
rationale: The sweetness of light and seeing the sun contrasts with the approaching darkening of sun, light, moon and stars in the closing portrayal of decline.

relationship: progression from enjoyment to difficult years
rationale: The source joins rejoicing over many years with remembering dark days; the following chapter anticipates years in which the aging person has no desire.
The source bounds youthful enjoyment with God's coming judgment; the conclusion repeats that every deed, good or evil, enters that judgment.

relationship: parallel removal of anger and evil
rationale: The source commands removing anger and putting away evil; James similarly combines slowness to anger with putting away impurity and abundant evil.
Remembering the Creator during youth complements the preceding invitation to youthful gladness that is explicitly bounded by awareness of God's judgment.
The darkening heavenly lights reverse the earlier delight in light and seeing the sun, forming a contrast between present vitality and coming decline.

relationship: comparison of decline with a contrasting hope
rationale: Shaken keepers, bent strength and failing sight portray decline within the source's mortality poem; Paul acknowledges the outer person's wasting while adding inward renewal. No exact bodily decoding of each image is claimed.
The source sends the human being to an everlasting home amid mourners; the psalm explicitly describes tombs as people's houses for ever.
Broken vessels and disrupted mechanisms lead into the following declaration of dust returning to earth and spirit to God, placing the images within mortality without assigning them specific organs.

relationship: reversal of creation's dust and breath
rationale: The source returns dust to earth and spirit to its giver; Genesis describes God forming the human from earth's dust and imparting life's breath.
The concluding futility declaration repeats the opening formula and its attribution to Ecclesiastes, closing the book's principal frame.

Ecclesiastes teaches knowledge, and the unit mentions an orderly arrangement of proverbs; Proverbs similarly introduces a collection intended to teach wisdom, understanding and interpretation of sayings.
The search for delightful and upright words compares with Proverbs' precious-ornament image for spoken speech; the comparison concerns valued expression, not identical claims about truth.

relationship: shared fastening imagery for wise speech
rationale: Wise words are planted nails in the source; Proverbs pictures a wise word fitting a receptive ear as a precious stone fastened in a golden earring.
The warning that much study wearies the flesh recalls the opening observation that increasing knowledge increases pain.
The source summarizes human duty as fearing God and keeping His commandments; Deuteronomy likewise describes God's requirement through fear, service and commandment-keeping.

relationship: parallel judgment of good and evil deeds
rationale: Both bring human deeds, whether good or evil, into comprehensive divine judgment; Paul identifies the judgment seat as Christ's.
